question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear combination of all SNPs (i.e., the population-level multiple regression of the phenotype on the SNP matrix). A polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates; even when every SNP is included and LD is perfect, sampling error, winner’s-curse bias, and imperfect tagging ensure that the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples—an unattainable condition in any real analysis. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

(The statement would be false only if “necessarily” were replaced by “typically” or if the question referred to the theoretical upper bound rather than an actual PGS.)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all SNPs (in aggregate) under the assumption of perfect knowledge of their effects. A polygenic score (PGS) is a finite linear combination of estimated SNP effects; as the discovery-sample size grows without bound, those estimates converge to the true effects, so the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS can asymptotically reach (but need not fall short of) \(h^2_{SNP}\). The qualifier “necessarily” is therefore false.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and thus in principle predictable from) the set of SNPs used in the heritability analysis. A polygenic score constructed from those same SNPs, with effect sizes estimated without error (e.g., in the infinite-sample limit), would therefore achieve an out-of-sample R² exactly equal to the SNP heritability. In finite samples the achieved R² is lower because of estimation error, but the inequality is not necessary; equality is attainable asymptotically. Hence the statement is false.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of variance that can be explained by SNPs (i.e., an upper bound on additive genetic prediction from the observed variants). A polygenic score constructed from the true effect sizes of those SNPs would achieve an out-of-sample R² exactly equal to this quantity; any gap observed in practice arises only from estimation error, incomplete variant coverage, or other methodological limitations, not from a mathematical necessity that R² must be strictly lower. Therefore the claim is false.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total additive variance tagged by the measured SNPs (an upper bound on what any linear combination of those SNPs can explain). A PGS is simply one particular linear combination whose weights are estimated from finite data; with infinite discovery-sample size the weights converge to the true causal effects and the out-of-sample \(R^2\) therefore converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the PGS \(R^2\) is bounded above by, but is not necessarily strictly below, SNP heritability.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the optimal linear predictor constructed from all SNPs (i.e., the squared correlation between the phenotype and its projection onto the space spanned by the SNPs). A polygenic score is a plug-in estimator of that linear predictor whose SNP weights are obtained from finite-sample GWAS summary statistics. Because those weights contain estimation error (sampling noise, imperfect LD tagging, winner’s curse, etc.), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any realizable PGS is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the unattainable limit of infinite GWAS samples and perfect knowledge of causal effects would equality hold; under all practical conditions the inequality is therefore strict. Hence the statement is true.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear predictor that uses all SNPs (i.e., the squared correlation between the phenotype and the true additive genetic scores). A polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample, noisy estimates of those SNP effects; the resulting predictor is therefore a suboptimal approximation to the best linear predictor. Consequently its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) (although it can approach \(h^2_{SNP}\) asymptotically as sample size grows and estimation error vanishes). This inequality is a direct statistical consequence of using estimated rather than population quantities, so the statement holds.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by all SNPs together (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on additive SNP-based prediction). A polygenic score, however, is formed from finite-sample effect-size estimates; those estimates contain sampling noise, winner’s-curse bias, and possible pruning or regularization. Consequently the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any practicable PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the idealized limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data would equality be reached; under all realistic conditions the inequality is strict.

Final answer: True
